partText: (a) Define force.
B_keywords: rate of change of momentum|change in momentum per unit time|change in momentum per second|change of momentum per unit time|momentum change per unit time|change in momentum / time|change in momentum/time|change of momentum / time|rate of momentum change|dp/dt|Δp/Δt|Δp/t|change in momentum divided by time|change in momentum over time
modelAnswer: Force is the rate of change of momentum.
explanation: Newton’s second law in its general form: force = rate of change of momentum.

partText: (b) Show that the SI base units of force are kg m s−2.
modelAnswer: momentum = kg m s⁻¹, so force = (kg m s⁻¹) / s = kg m s⁻²
explanation: Momentum = mass × velocity has base units kg m s⁻¹. Dividing by time (s) gives kg m s⁻².

partText:
(c) A student is investigating the relationship between the force applied to the piston of a syringe and the velocity of fluid exiting the syringe. The student wishes to use the equation

v = Fk / (mA)

where:
v is the velocity of fluid exiting the syringe
F is the force applied to the piston
k is a constant with SI base units ${kunit}
m is the mass of the fluid in the syringe
A is the cross-sectional area of the piston.

By considering SI base units on both sides of the equation, state and explain whether this equation is homogeneous.
modelAnswer: (Base units of) F = kg m s⁻², m = kg, A = m². RHS = kg m s⁻² × ${kunit} / (kg m²) = ${rhs}. ${concl}.
explanation: Write each quantity in base units: F = kg m s⁻², m = kg, A = m². Substitute into Fk/(mA) and simplify, then compare with the base units of v (m s⁻¹).

partText: (a) State the principle of conservation of momentum.
B_keywords: [["total momentum", "sum of the momenta", "sum of momentum", "momentum of a system", "momentum of the system", "momentum before", "total linear momentum", "momentum of the objects", "momentum of the bodies", "momentum of an isolated"], ["constant", "conserved", "same", "unchanged", "equal", "remains", "does not change", "stays", "after", "="]]
B2_keywords: isolated|closed system|no external force|no resultant external force|no resultant force|no net external force|no net force|no external forces|without external force|without any external force|no outside force
modelAnswer: The total momentum of a system of interacting bodies remains constant (before = after), provided no resultant external force acts on the system (isolated system).
explanation: Linear momentum is conserved in any interaction when the system is isolated, i.e. when there is no resultant external force.

partText:
(b)(i) A boat of mass ${M} kg is at rest on the surface of water. A sack of mass ${m} kg is thrown horizontally with a speed of ${u} m s−1 towards the mast of the boat, as shown in Figure 2.1.${f21}The sack sticks to the mast. Frictional forces between the boat and the water are negligible.

Calculate the speed of the boat immediately after the sack sticks to the mast.
modelAnswer: conservation of momentum: ${m} × ${u} = (${M} + ${m}) × v, so v = ${vs} m s⁻¹
explanation: The sack and the boat move together after the collision, so their total mass is ${Mt} kg. Momentum is conserved because there is no resultant horizontal external force.

partText:
(b)(ii) Determine the ratio

kinetic energy of the boat and sack after the collision / kinetic energy of the sack before the collision.
modelAnswer: E before = ½ × ${m} × ${u}² = ${KEb_2} J;  E after = ½ × ${Mt} × ${vd}² = ${KEa_2} J;  ratio = ${rats}
explanation: Use E = ½mv² for each situation. After the collision the moving mass is the boat and sack together (${Mt} kg); before the collision it is the sack alone (${m} kg).

partText: (b)(iii) State and explain whether the collision between the sack and the boat is elastic or inelastic.
B_keywords: [["inelastic"], ["kineticenergy", "kinetic energy", "ke", "energy", "e2", "e1", "speed of approach", "relative speed", "speed of separation", "less", "lost", "decrease", "reduced", "converted", "transferred"]]
modelAnswer: The collision is inelastic because the kinetic energy after the collision is less than the kinetic energy before it (the ratio in (b)(ii) is less than 1).
explanation: In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy is conserved. Here the sack and boat move off together (no relative speed of separation) and the total kinetic energy has decreased.

partText:
(c)(i) The boat with the sack on board floats at rest on the water.

Show that the upthrust acting on the boat and sack is ${Fus} N.
modelAnswer: The boat and sack are in equilibrium so upthrust = weight = (${M} + ${m}) × 9.81 = ${Fud} N = ${Fus} N (2 s.f.)
explanation: The boat and sack float at rest, so the resultant force is zero: the upthrust is equal to the total weight, (M + m)g.

partText:
(c)(ii) The volume of water displaced by the boat and sack is ${Vsci} cm3.

Determine the density of the water. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
modelAnswer: ρ = m / V = ${Mt} / (${Vsci} × 10⁻⁶) = ${dens_s} kg m⁻³  (equivalently: upthrust = ρVg)
explanation: The upthrust equals the weight of the water displaced, ρVg, and also equals the weight of the boat and sack. Convert cm³ to m³ (1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³) before calculating.

partText:
(a)(i) A rollercoaster carriage of mass ${m} kg moves along a track from X to Y, and then to Z, as shown in Figure 3.1.${f31}Point Z is at the same height as point X. The carriage has kinetic energy ${KEx} kJ at X and ${KEy} kJ at Y. The length of the track between X and Y is ${s} m. The work done against resistive forces between X and Y is ${Wk} kJ.

Calculate the average resistive force acting on the carriage between X and Y.
modelAnswer: work done = force × distance, so F = ${Wk} × 10³ / ${s} = ${Fs} N
explanation: The work done against the resistive forces is the force multiplied by the distance moved along the track. Convert kJ to J before dividing.

partText: (a)(ii) Determine the vertical height Δh between X and Y.
modelAnswer: energy converted to gravitational potential energy = ${KEx} − ${KEy} − ${Wk} = ${Ep} kJ;  E = mgΔh, so Δh = ${Epj} / (${m} × 9.81) = ${dhs} m
explanation: Energy is conserved: the loss of kinetic energy from X to Y is shared between the work done against resistive forces and the gain in gravitational potential energy.

partText: (b) State and explain how the speed of the carriage at Z compares with its speed at X.
modelAnswer: The speed at Z is less than the speed at X: Z is at the same height as X, but work is done against resistive forces, so the kinetic energy (and therefore the speed) is less.
explanation: X and Z are at the same height, so there is no net change in gravitational potential energy. Energy is transferred to thermal energy by the resistive forces, so the kinetic energy at Z is less than at X.

partText: (a)(i) State what is meant by the moment of a force.
modelAnswer: The moment of a force is the force × the perpendicular distance from the pivot (point) to the line of action of the force.
explanation: Moment = force × perpendicular distance between the line of action of the force and the pivot (or point) about which the moment is taken.

partText:
(a)(ii) A picture hangs on a wall from a pin P using a wire, as shown in Figure 4.1.${f41}The weight of the picture is ${Wn} N. The tension in each side of the wire is ${T} N.

Explain why the weight of the picture has zero moment about P.
B_keywords: perpendicular distance is zero|perpendicular distance=0|perpendicular distance of zero|distance is zero|distance of zero|zero perpendicular distance|zero distance|no perpendicular distance|line of action passes through p|line of action goes through p|line of action through p|line of action of the weight passes|acts through p|passes through p|through the pin|through pin p|acts through the pin|acts at p|weight acts through p|acts directly below p|is directly below p|directly below p|vertically below p|in line with p|p is on the line of action|pivot is on the line of action|pin is on the line of action
modelAnswer: The line of action of the weight passes through P (the weight acts vertically below P), so the perpendicular distance from P to the line of action is zero.
explanation: Moment = force × perpendicular distance. The weight acts vertically downwards through the centre of gravity, which is directly below P, so the perpendicular distance from P is zero.

partText: (a)(iii) Determine the angle θ shown in Figure 4.1.
modelAnswer: vertical forces balance: 2T sinθ = W, so sinθ = ${Wn} / (2 × ${T}) = ${sns}, θ = ${ths}°
explanation: The picture is in equilibrium, so the vertical components of the two tensions balance the weight: 2T sinθ = W.

partText:
(a)(iv) The wire has a circular cross-section of diameter ${ds} mm and a Young modulus of ${Ei} × 1010 Pa.

Calculate the strain in the wire.
modelAnswer: A = πd²/4 = ${Aw_c} m²;  stress = F / A = ${T} / ${Aw_c} = ${sg_c} Pa;  strain = stress / E = ${eps_c}
explanation: Strain = stress / Young modulus (E = stress / strain). The stress is the tension divided by the cross-sectional area of the wire; the diameter must be converted to metres before the area is found.

partText:
(b)(i) The picture falls from rest. The bottom of the picture is ${h} m above the ground. Air resistance is negligible.

Calculate the time taken for the bottom of the picture to reach the ground.
explanation: The picture falls freely from rest with acceleration g, so s = ut + ½at² with u = 0.

partText: (b)(ii) Which sketch shows how the speed of the bottom of the picture varies with the distance it has fallen, from 0 to ${h} m? All the sketches use the same axes.
modelAnswer: A curve starting at the origin whose gradient is positive and continuously decreasing (v = √(2gs)).
explanation: For constant acceleration from rest, v² = 2gs, so v = √(2gs): the graph of v against s passes through the origin and its gradient decreases continuously.

partText: (a)(i) Define the period of an oscillation.
B_keywords: time for one oscillation|time for one complete oscillation|time taken for one oscillation|time taken for one complete oscillation|time for one cycle|time taken for one cycle|time for one complete cycle|time taken for one complete cycle|time of one oscillation|time of one cycle|time to complete one oscillation|time to complete one cycle|time for one wave|time for one complete wave|time taken for one complete wave|time for a complete oscillation|time for a complete cycle|time taken for a complete oscillation|time taken for a complete cycle|one complete oscillation|one complete cycle|1/f|1/frequency|reciprocal of frequency|time taken to complete one
modelAnswer: The period is the time taken for one complete oscillation (cycle).
explanation: The period T is the time for one complete cycle of the oscillation; it is the reciprocal of the frequency, T = 1/f.

partText: (a)(ii) Define the amplitude of an oscillation.
B_keywords: maximum displacement|max displacement|greatest displacement|largest displacement|maximum distance from equilibrium|maximum distance from the equilibrium|maximum distance from the mean|maximum distance from rest|maximum distance from the rest|greatest distance from equilibrium|greatest distance from the equilibrium|greatest distance from the mean|maximum distance from the equilibrium position|maximum distance from the mean position|distance from the equilibrium position to the maximum|maximum displacement from the equilibrium|maximum displacement from the mean|maximum displacement from the rest|maximum displacement from the equilibrium position|biggest displacement
modelAnswer: The amplitude is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium (mean) position.
explanation: Amplitude is the largest displacement of the oscillating particle from its equilibrium position.

partText: (b)(i) A stationary wave is formed on a string that is fixed at both ends. Each sketch shows the string at an instant when it has its maximum displacement, with a cross (×) drawn at one position on the string. Which sketch shows the cross at the position of an antinode?
modelAnswer: The cross is at a point of maximum amplitude, half-way between two adjacent nodes (at the peak or trough of a loop).
explanation: Antinodes are the points of maximum amplitude on a stationary wave. Nodes are the points where the string never moves.

partText:
(b)(ii) The stationary wave in (b)(i) has a frequency of ${f} Hz. The distance between the two fixed ends of the string is ${Ls} m.

Show that the speed of progressive waves on the string is ${vs} m s−1.
modelAnswer: there are 1.5 wavelengths (three loops) between the fixed ends, so λ = 2 × ${Ls} / 3 = ${lams} m;  v = fλ = ${f} × ${lams} = ${vs} m s⁻¹
explanation: Each loop is half a wavelength. Three loops give 3λ/2 = ${Ls} m, so λ = 2 × ${Ls} / 3. Then use v = fλ.

partText:
(b)(iii) The frequency of the vibration generator is now increased to ${f2} Hz. The speed of progressive waves on the string does not change.

Determine whether a stationary wave is formed on the string at this frequency.
B2_keywords: [["not", "no stationary", "no standing", "cannot", "wont", "isnt", "isn’t", "never", "nostationary"], ["whole number", "integer", "half wavelengths", "half-wavelengths", "half wavelength", "nodes", "2l/n", "l=nλ/2", "nλ/2", "not a multiple", "multiple", "fit", "harmonic", "resonan", "λ/2", "n=${nhs}", "${nhs}", "n =", "non-integer", "fraction", "decimal"]]
modelAnswer: λ = v / f = ${vs} / ${f2} = ${lam2s} m. A stationary wave needs a whole number of half-wavelengths on the string: L / (λ/2) = 2 × ${Ls} / ${lam2s} = ${nhs}, which is not a whole number, so a stationary wave is not formed.
explanation: A stationary wave forms on a string fixed at both ends only when the length of the string is a whole number of half-wavelengths, L = nλ/2. At ${f2} Hz this does not happen.

partText: (c)(i) Light of wavelength ${lg} × 10−7 m is incident normally on a diffraction grating. The grating has ${Ng} × 105 lines per metre. A bright spot X is observed on a screen at an angle of ${thr}° to the straight-through direction, as shown in Figure 5.1.${fg}Determine the order n of the bright spot X.
modelAnswer: d = 1 / (${Ng} × 10⁵) = ${dg_c} m;  d sinθ = nλ, so n = ${dg_c} × sin ${thr}° / (${lg} × 10⁻⁷) = ${ni}
explanation: For a diffraction grating, d sinθ = nλ, where the line spacing d is the reciprocal of the number of lines per metre. The order n must be a whole number.

partText:
(c)(ii) The diffraction grating is replaced by a grating with fewer lines per metre. The positions of the grating and the screen, and the light, are unchanged.

State how the distance between adjacent bright spots on the screen changes.
modelAnswer: The distance between adjacent bright spots decreases.
explanation: Fewer lines per metre means a larger line spacing d. Since d sinθ = nλ, sinθ is smaller for a given order, so the spots move closer together.

partText: (a) Define electric current.
B_keywords: flow of charge|flow of charged particles|flow of electrons|flow of charge carriers|rate of flow of charge|rate of flow of charged|charge per unit time|charge per second|charge/time|charge flowing per|flow of ions|movement of charge|movement of electrons|movement of charged|flow of positive|flow of negative|moving charge|rate of change of charge|rate of charge flow|rate of flow of electrons|charge passing|charge flowing|Δq/Δt|dq/dt|q/t
modelAnswer: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge (flow of charge carriers).
explanation: Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = ΔQ / Δt. The charge carriers are electrons in a metal.

partText: (b) A cell has e.m.f. ${Es} V and internal resistance ${rs} Ω. Which sketch shows how the terminal potential difference of the cell varies with the current in the cell, for currents from 0 to 1.6 A? All the sketches use the same axes.
modelAnswer: A straight line with a negative gradient, starting at ${Es} V when the current is zero and reaching ${sf(E-1.6*r,2)} V at 1.60 A.
explanation: Terminal p.d. V = E − Ir. When I = 0, V = E = ${Es} V. When I = 1.6 A, V = ${Es} − 1.6 × ${rs} = ${sf(E-1.6*r,2)} V. The graph is a straight line of gradient −r.

partText:
(c)(i) A wire X has length ${Lw} m, cross-sectional area ${Aws} × 10−7 m2 and resistance ${Rws} Ω.

Calculate the resistivity of the material of wire X.
modelAnswer: R = ρL / A, so ρ = RA / L = ${Rws} × ${Aws} × 10⁻⁷ / ${Lw} = ${rho_c} Ω m
explanation: Use resistivity ρ = RA / L. The area is given in units of 10⁻⁷ m².

partText:
(c)(ii) Wire X is connected in parallel with a fixed resistor R to the cell, as shown in Figure 6.2.${f62}The current in the cell is ${Iss} A.

Calculate the resistance of the fixed resistor R.
modelAnswer: terminal p.d. = ${Es} − ${Iss} × ${rs} = ${Vts} V;  current in X = ${Vts} / ${Rws} = ${sf(Vt/Rw,2)} A;  current in R = ${Iss} − ${sf(Vt/Rw,2)} = ${IRs} A;  R = ${Vts} / ${IRs} = ${Ra_s} Ω
explanation: The p.d. across R and X is the terminal p.d. of the cell, V = E − Ir. The current in X is V / R<sub>X</sub>. The current in R is the cell current minus the current in X.

partText: (c)(iii) Calculate the power dissipated in the internal resistance of the cell.
modelAnswer: P = I²r = ${Iss}² × ${rs} = ${P_s} W
explanation: The power dissipated in the internal resistance is I²r, using the current in the cell, because the internal resistance is in series with the external circuit.

partText: (a) Describe the structure of a nuclear atom.
B_keywords: [["nucleus", "nuclei"], ["protons and neutrons", "neutrons and protons", "proton and neutron", "neutron and proton", "nucleons", "protons, neutrons", "protons neutrons", "neutrons protons", "proton neutron", "neutron proton", "protons & neutrons", "neutrons & protons", "protons+neutrons", "protons plus neutrons", "neutrons, protons"]]
modelAnswer: A (small, dense) nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by (orbiting) electrons.
explanation: Almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in the small central nucleus, which contains protons and neutrons (nucleons); the electrons orbit the nucleus.

partText:
(b)(i) Nucleus P has ${ZP} protons. Nucleus P decays by emitting a single particle to form a nucleus with ${Zt} protons.

State the name of the particle emitted by nucleus P.
modelAnswer: ${nameP} (particle)
explanation: The proton number changes from ${ZP} to ${Zt}, a change of ${Zt-ZP}. Only the ${nameP} decay changes the proton number in this way.

partText:
(b)(ii) Nucleus Q has ${ZQ} protons. Nucleus Q decays by emitting a single particle to form a nucleus with ${Zt} protons.

State the name of the particle emitted by nucleus Q.
modelAnswer: ${nameQ} (particle)
explanation: The proton number changes from ${ZQ} to ${Zt}, a change of ${Zt-ZQ}. Only the ${nameQ} decay changes the proton number in this way.

partText:
(c) A particle X has a charge-to-mass ratio of +${ratt} C kg−1. The charge on X is ${qtxt}.

Determine the mass of X and hence identify X.
modelAnswer: mass = charge / (charge-to-mass ratio) = ${qc} × 10⁻¹⁹ / (${ratt}) = ${mass_c} kg;  X is a ${pname}
explanation: Mass = charge ÷ (charge-to-mass ratio). Compare the mass found with the masses of the electron (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) and the proton (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg); X has a positive charge.
